title: The Protocols: Anatomy of a Forgery
bigQuestion: How can a careful reader prove that a document is a forgery, and why can a proven lie keep doing harm?

story.title: An Old Book in Constantinople
story.kicker: In 1921 a British reporter is handed a worn French book and finds the famous secret plan already inside it.
paragraphs: It is the summer of 1921 in Constantinople, the great city on the Bosporus now called Istanbul. Philip Graves is the correspondent there for The Times of London. The city is crowded with people who fled the Russian Revolution and civil war. Some of them bring stories. Some bring papers. One of them brings Graves a book.

The man is a Russian exile. In his articles Graves calls him only Mr. X. Historians later identified him as Mikhail Raslovlev. He hands over an old French book, worn from use, and says something strange. Read this, he tells Graves, and then read the Protocols of the Elders of Zion.

Graves knows the Protocols. It is a pamphlet that claims to be the secret minutes of Jewish leaders plotting to rule the world. It has spread across Europe and America since the Russian Revolution. Many readers treat it as proof of a hidden plot. Even in Britain, some serious people have asked whether it might be real.

Graves reads the French book. It is a satire from 1864, written by a lawyer named Maurice Joly to mock a French emperor. It does not mention Jews at all. Yet page after page, its ideas and images match the Protocols, often in the same order. Graves begins to set the two texts side by side. In August 1921 The Times prints what he found.
story.think: Graves had a strong hunch, but he did not just announce it. Why was printing the two texts side by side more convincing than simply saying the Protocols were fake?

lessons.title: Joly's Satire of 1864
lessons.mainIdea: The Protocols copied a French satire from 1864 that attacked Emperor Napoleon III and never mentioned Jews.
reading: In 1864 a French lawyer named Maurice Joly published a book in Brussels, Belgium. He did not put his name on it. The title page said only that it was written by a contemporary, meaning someone living at the time. Its title in English is Dialogue in Hell Between Machiavelli and Montesquieu.

The book is a *satire*. A satire uses humor, irony or exaggeration to criticize real people or real power. Joly's target was Napoleon III, the emperor of France. Joly believed the emperor kept a free-looking government on the surface while controlling it underneath. He could not safely say that openly, because France had strict *censorship*, meaning government control over what could be printed.

So Joly wrote a *dialogue*, a text written as a conversation. Two dead thinkers argue in the afterlife. Montesquieu defends laws, liberty and a free press. Machiavelli explains, coldly and cleverly, how a modern ruler could control newspapers, courts and voters while pretending to respect them. Readers were meant to recognize Napoleon III in Machiavelli's plans.

The French government did recognize him. Joly was identified, tried and sentenced in April 1865 to 18 months in prison. His book was seized and soon forgotten. Keep one fact in mind for the rest of this chapter: Joly's satire is about a French emperor. It does not mention Jews at all.

words.d: writing that uses humor, irony or exaggeration to criticize real people or real power
government control over what may be printed, said or shown
a piece of writing set out as a conversation between speakers

look.title: Joly's Book, as the Catalog Records It
look.text: A dialogue in hell between Machiavelli and Montesquieu, or the politics of Machiavelli in the nineteenth century, by a contemporary. Printed in Brussels by A. Mertens and Sons, 1864.
look.cite: Maurice Joly, Dialogue aux enfers entre Machiavel et Montesquieu, Brussels: A. Mertens et fils, 1864 (title page, in English)
look.prompt: The title page does not name the author, and the book was printed outside France. What do these two choices suggest about the risks Joly faced?

check.q: Who was the real target of Joly's 1864 satire?
choices: Emperor Napoleon III of France
Tsar Nicholas II of Russia
The Jewish community of Paris
The pope in Rome
check.why: Joly wrote the Dialogue to criticize Napoleon III; readers were meant to see the emperor in Machiavelli's plans.

check.q: Why did Joly write his criticism as a conversation between two dead thinkers?
choices: Because he wanted to write a history of Italy
Because Montesquieu had asked him to
Because France had strict censorship and open criticism was risky
Because the book was meant for children
check.why: France controlled the press, so Joly hid his attack inside a satirical dialogue. He was still jailed for it.

check.q: Which statement about Joly's book is true?
choices: It describes a secret Jewish meeting
It never mentions Jews at all
It was first printed in Russia in 1903
It was praised by Napoleon III
check.why: Joly's satire is about a French emperor and does not mention Jews. That fact matters when we compare it to the Protocols.

lessons.title: A Forgery Appears in Russia
lessons.mainIdea: The Protocols was first printed in a St. Petersburg newspaper in 1903 and in a fuller book version in 1905.
reading: Nearly forty years after Joly's book, a new text appeared in the Russian Empire. In August and September of 1903, a St. Petersburg newspaper called Znamya, meaning The Banner, printed it in parts. The paper's editor was Pavel Krushevan, a writer known for his hostility toward Jews. The text later became known as the Protocols of the Elders of Zion.

A *protocol* here means the official minutes of a meeting. The text claims to be the secret minutes of Jewish leaders planning to take over the world. It is a *forgery*: a document made to look like something it is not, in order to deceive. No such meeting took place, and no such leaders existed.

In 1905 a religious writer named Sergei Nilus printed a fuller version as the last chapter of a book of his. Nilus's edition became the one most often translated. The timing matters. The Russian Empire was a place of deep *antisemitism*, meaning hatred of or prejudice against Jews. In those years mobs carried out deadly attacks on Jewish communities, called pogroms. A forgery like this did not create hatred from nothing. It fed on fears that already existed and gave them the look of proof. That is why historians study not only who wrote a false document, but also who wanted to believe it.

words.d: here, the official written minutes of a meeting
a document made to look like something it is not, in order to deceive
hatred of, or prejudice against, Jewish people
a violent mob attack on a Jewish community, especially in the Russian Empire

look.title: From Satire to Forgery: Key Years
look.cite: Joly (1864); Znamya, St. Petersburg (1903); S. Nilus (1905); P. Graves, The Times, 16-18 Aug. 1921
look.prompt: How many years passed between Joly's satire and the first printing of the Protocols? How might that gap have helped the forgers?

check.q: Where was the Protocols first printed?
choices: In The Times of London in 1921
In a Brussels book in 1864
In a Chicago newspaper in 1920
In a St. Petersburg newspaper in 1903
check.why: The reading says Znamya, a St. Petersburg paper edited by Pavel Krushevan, printed it in 1903.

check.q: In this chapter, what is a forgery?
choices: A true record that was later lost
A satire that openly mocks a ruler
A translation of an older book
A document made to look like something it is not, in order to deceive
check.why: A forgery is made to deceive. The Protocols pretends to be secret minutes of a meeting that never happened.

check.q: According to the reading, why did the Protocols find believers in the Russian Empire?
choices: It fed on antisemitic fears that already existed
It was signed by famous leaders
It was sold as a comic novel
The government had tested it in court
check.why: The reading says the forgery fed on existing hatred and gave it the look of proof.

lessons.title: Who Made It? An Open Question
lessons.mainIdea: Historians agree the Protocols is a forgery, but they still debate exactly who made it.
reading: Students often ask who wrote the Protocols. The honest answer is that historians are not sure. There is a difference between two questions. Is the text a forgery? That question is settled. Who forged it? That question is still open, and historians argue about it using evidence.

The traditional view points to the Okhrana, the secret police of the Russian tsar, and its office in Paris. The historian Norman Cohn, in his 1967 book Warrant for Genocide, followed this view, which rests partly on witnesses who spoke at a trial in the 1930s. In 1999 a Russian scholar, Mikhail Lepekhin, named a writer called Mathieu Golovinski as the author. That claim is disputed.

Other historians look elsewhere. Cesare De Michelis, in a 2004 study, argued that the text came from Russian nationalist circles around 1902 and 1903. Scholars also agree that the forger borrowed from more than one source. One was an 1868 German novel by Hermann Goedsche, which included an invented scene of a secret meeting in a Prague cemetery.

This is a good example of how a *historian* works. A historian studies the past using evidence and says how sure each claim is. We can hold two ideas at once. We know the Protocols is fake because of what it copies. We do not yet know for certain whose hands did the copying. An open question about the author does not reopen the question of the forgery.

words.d: the secret police of the Russian tsars before 1917
a person who studies the past using evidence and says how sure each claim is
a claim about who made or wrote something

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim A: The Protocols copies long passages from Joly's 1864 satire. Claim B: The Russian secret police in Paris produced the Protocols. Claim C: Mathieu Golovinski wrote the Protocols. Claim D: The Protocols records a real secret meeting of Jewish leaders.
look.prompt: Label each claim as settled by evidence, still debated by historians, or shown false. For one claim, name the evidence that decides it.

check.q: Which question about the Protocols is settled?
choices: Exactly which person wrote it
Which office of the secret police paid for it
Whether it is a forgery
Whether Golovinski was the author
check.why: The reading says that the forgery is settled, while the identity of the forger is still debated.

check.q: What did Cesare De Michelis argue in 2004?
choices: That the Protocols was genuine
That the text came from Russian nationalist circles around 1902 and 1903
That Joly wrote the Protocols himself
That Graves invented the whole story
check.why: De Michelis argued for Russian nationalist circles, a different view from the traditional secret police account.

check.q: Besides Joly, which other source did the forger borrow from, according to scholars?
choices: An 1868 German novel by Hermann Goedsche
A speech by Napoleon III
Minutes of the Bern court
A 1920 Ford newspaper article
check.why: Scholars agree that Goedsche's 1868 novel, with its invented Prague cemetery scene, was also used.

lessons.title: The Times Prints the Proof
lessons.mainIdea: In August 1921 Philip Graves showed in The Times that the Protocols had been copied from Joly's satire.
reading: Philip Graves was a careful British journalist based in Constantinople. After Mr. X gave him Joly's book, Graves compared it with the Protocols line by line. He found that the Protocols had borrowed Joly's arguments, images and order of ideas. The forger had changed the speaker. In Joly, it is Machiavelli advising a ruler. In the Protocols, it is the supposed Jewish elders.

The Times printed Graves's findings in three articles on 16, 17 and 18 August 1921. The paper then reissued them as a pamphlet with a plain title: The Truth About the Protocols: A Literary Forgery. A *literary forgery* is a fake that is built by copying and changing someone else's writing.

This mattered because of who was speaking. The Times was one of the most respected newspapers in the world. The year before, some voices in Britain had asked whether the Protocols might be genuine. Now the same paper laid out the *evidence* for readers to judge. Evidence is the facts or documents that show whether a claim is true. Graves did not ask readers to trust him. He showed them the two texts together. That choice turned a debate about opinions into a test anyone could check with their own eyes.

words.d: a reporter who sends news from a particular place, often abroad
a fake text built by copying and changing someone else's writing
facts or documents that show whether a claim is true

look.title: What Graves Reported
look.text: Graves reported that the Protocols was largely a clumsy copy of Joly's 1864 satire on Napoleon III. The forger kept Joly's arguments and their order, and replaced the French emperor's methods with a supposed Jewish plan.
look.cite: Philip Graves, The Truth About 'The Protocols': A Literary Forgery, from The Times (London), 16, 17 and 18 August 1921
look.prompt: Graves's finding has two parts: what was kept and what was changed. Why are both parts important for proving a forgery?

check.q: When did The Times print Graves's articles?
choices: May 1935
August 1903
16-18 August 1921
June 1927
check.why: The reading gives 16, 17 and 18 August 1921 as the dates of the three articles.

check.q: What did the forger change when copying Joly?
choices: The language, from Russian to French
The speaker, from Machiavelli to supposed Jewish elders
The ending, so that Montesquieu wins
Nothing; the texts are identical
check.why: Graves showed that the forger kept Joly's arguments but put them in the mouths of invented Jewish elders.

check.q: Why did it matter that The Times published this exposure?
choices: It was the only paper in Constantinople
It owned the rights to Joly's book
It was run by the Russian government
It was a respected paper, and some voices in Britain had taken the Protocols seriously
check.why: The reading says The Times was widely respected, which gave the evidence a large and serious audience.

lessons.title: Reading in Parallel Columns
lessons.mainIdea: Setting two texts side by side lets any reader see copied structure, wording and order.
reading: Graves used a simple tool: *parallel columns*. He printed a passage from Joly on one side and the matching passage from the Protocols on the other. Readers could move their eyes back and forth. They did not need to know French or Russian history. They only needed to compare.

What should a reader look for? First, the order of ideas. Two authors writing on their own might share one idea, but they will rarely share twenty ideas in the same order. Second, distinctive images, such as an unusual comparison or example. Third, small leftovers: details that made sense in the original but look odd in the copy.

This lesson uses an invented, harmless example so the method is clear. In the practice below, one text is an original school newsletter and the other copies it. You will not read the Protocols itself. That text was written to spread hatred. Historians who teach it show only short matching lines, and only to prove the copying. When a match is long, detailed and in the same order, chance is not a reasonable explanation. The newer text depends on the older one. That is called *textual dependence*. It is one of the strongest kinds of proof a historian can offer.

words.d: two texts printed side by side so readers can compare them line by line
proof that one text was built from another, shown by shared wording, images and order
unusual enough to stand out and be recognized

look.title: Practice: Two Newsletters
look.text: Original (a school newsletter, March): Our garden is a small country. The tomatoes are its citizens, the fence is its border, and the hose is its only road. Copy (a flyer found in April): The club is a small country. Its members are its citizens, its rules are its border, and the hose is its only road.
look.prompt: List three things the flyer kept from the newsletter. Which leftover detail gives the copy away, and why does it look odd in the new text?

check.q: What are parallel columns?
choices: Columns of numbers in a budget
A kind of secret code
Pillars in a lodge building
Two texts printed side by side for comparison
check.why: Graves printed Joly and the Protocols side by side so readers could compare them line by line.

check.q: Why is the same order of many ideas strong evidence of copying?
choices: Because two independent authors rarely share many ideas in the same sequence
Because all authors write in the same order
Because order is the only thing a forger cannot change
Because courts only accept evidence about order
check.why: The reading says independent writers might share one idea, but rarely twenty in the same order.

check.q: In the practice flyer, which detail is a leftover from the original?
choices: The club
Its members
The hose is its only road
Its rules are its border
check.why: A hose makes sense in a garden but not in a club, so it is a leftover from the newsletter being copied.

lessons.title: What the Copying Proves
lessons.mainIdea: Because the Protocols copies a satire about a French emperor, it cannot be the real record of a Jewish meeting.
reading: Proof of copying leads to a clear conclusion. Suppose the Protocols were real minutes of a secret meeting. Then the speakers' words would be their own. But the words are Joly's, written in 1864 to mock Napoleon III. A real meeting could not have produced a speech that already existed, word for word in places, in a French satire.

The copy also carries odd leftovers. Some are an *anachronism*, something placed in the wrong time. Scholars have noted passages that fit France under Napoleon III better than the world of 1903, because that is what Joly was writing about. A forger working fast did not clean every trace.

The deeper point is about blame. Joly's satire was a warning about how any ruler could abuse power. The forger took that warning and pinned it on a whole people who had nothing to do with it. That is what made the forgery so dangerous. It turned a general fear of power into hatred of a specific group. Notice what the proof does not need. It does not depend on who the forger was or on anyone's opinion of Jews. It rests on the texts themselves. Anyone can check it. That is why historians call the question closed.

words.d: something placed in a time where it does not belong
a person or group unfairly blamed for problems they did not cause
a judgment reached by reasoning from evidence

look.title: A Chain of Reasoning
look.text: Step 1: Joly's satire was printed in 1864 and attacks Napoleon III. Step 2: The Protocols first appeared in 1903. Step 3: Long parts of the Protocols match Joly in wording, images and order. Step 4: Therefore the Protocols depends on Joly.
look.prompt: Add a Step 5 that explains why the Protocols cannot be the real minutes of a secret meeting. Which step would a defender of the Protocols have to prove wrong?

check.q: What is an anachronism?
choices: A hidden message in a text
Something placed in a time where it does not belong
A second copy of a document
A kind of court ruling
check.why: An anachronism is something out of its proper time, like details about Napoleon III's France in a text claiming to be from 1903.

check.q: Why can the Protocols not be the record of a real meeting?
choices: Because its words were already written by Joly in 1864 to mock a French emperor
Because it is too short
Because it was first printed in Russian
Because no one read it before 1921
check.why: A real meeting could not produce speeches already written decades earlier in a satire about Napoleon III.

check.q: According to the reading, what made the forgery especially dangerous?
choices: It revealed real government secrets
It was written by a famous author
It turned a warning about any ruler into hatred of a specific people
It was hard to find in libraries
check.why: The forger pinned Joly's general warning about power on Jews, making them a scapegoat.

lessons.title: The Bern Trial
lessons.mainIdea: In 1935 a Swiss court in Bern ruled that the Protocols were forgeries, and a 1937 appeal did not change that finding.
reading: In the 1930s, pro-Nazi groups in Switzerland handed out copies of the Protocols. Swiss Jewish organizations went to court in Bern, the Swiss capital. They argued that the pamphlets broke a Bern law against trashy literature. The trial ran from October 1934 to May 1935, and witnesses testified about where the text came from.

On 14 May 1935, Judge Walter Meyer gave his ruling. He found the Protocols to be forgeries and called them trashy literature. Two of the five men charged, named Fischer and Schnell, were convicted. The other three were *acquitted*, meaning found not guilty.

The defendants made an *appeal*, asking a higher court to review the case. On 1 November 1937 the appeals court overturned the convictions. Its reason was a point of law: it held that the trashy literature statute did not fit a political text like this one. The appeals court did not rule that the Protocols were genuine. Later promoters of the Protocols sometimes say the Bern verdict was overturned, as if that proved the text real. That is a misreading. A *verdict* can be reversed because a law does not apply, while the facts found about a document still stand.

words.d: a court's decision in a case
found not guilty by a court
a request for a higher court to review a lower court's decision

look.title: The Bern Verdict, 14 May 1935
look.cite: Bern trial records, verdicts of 14 May 1935 and 1 November 1937 (EHRI archival description)
look.prompt: Only two of five men were convicted, and the appeal later overturned those convictions too. Does either fact tell us the Protocols might be real? Explain.

check.q: What did Judge Walter Meyer find in May 1935?
choices: That the Protocols were genuine minutes
That the Protocols were forgeries and trashy literature
That Joly had been a Russian spy
That the case should be sent to Russia
check.why: Meyer's verdict of 14 May 1935 found the Protocols to be forgeries and trashy literature.

check.q: Why did the appeals court overturn the convictions in 1937?
choices: It found new proof the Protocols were real
The judge had died
Graves withdrew his articles
It held that the trashy literature law did not fit the text
check.why: The appeal turned on a point of law. The court did not find the Protocols genuine.

check.q: What does acquitted mean?
choices: Sent to a higher court
Found guilty
Asked to testify
Found not guilty
check.why: Acquitted means found not guilty. Three of the five men in Bern were acquitted in 1935.

lessons.title: Henry Ford's Newspaper
lessons.mainIdea: Beginning in 1920, Henry Ford's Dearborn Independent spread the Protocols to a huge audience in America and abroad.
reading: Henry Ford was one of the most admired men in America. His Model T put millions of families on the road. He also owned a weekly newspaper, the Dearborn Independent, based in Dearborn, Michigan. On 22 May 1920 the paper began a series of attacks on Jews, and it kept them up in 91 more issues.

The series leaned heavily on the Protocols. It presented the forgery as a key to world events. The articles were then collected into books under the title The International Jew. The first volume appeared in November 1920. Ford's fame gave the old Russian forgery an American voice and a huge new audience.

This is a lesson about *propaganda*, meaning information spread on purpose to shape what people believe, often by misleading them. Propaganda works better when a trusted figure spreads it. Many readers reasoned that a man as successful as Ford must know what he was talking about. His success in business had nothing to do with whether the Protocols were true. The International Jew was translated into at least 16 languages, according to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. It traveled far beyond Michigan, including to Germany, where Nazi leaders praised it.

words.d: information spread on purpose to shape beliefs, often by misleading people
a set of related articles printed one after another
the quality of being trusted and believed

look.title: Ford's Paper and the Forgery
rows: Series begins in the Dearborn Independent
look.cite: The Dearborn Independent (1920-1927); The Times (London), Aug. 1921; Ford statement of 30 June 1927
look.prompt: Graves's proof appeared in 1921. For how many years after that did Ford's paper keep running? What does this tell you about whether debunking alone stops a lie?

check.q: When did the Dearborn Independent begin its series attacking Jews?
choices: May 1920
August 1921
June 1927
May 1935
check.why: The series began in the 22 May 1920 issue and ran in 91 more issues.

check.q: What is propaganda?
choices: A court ruling on a document
A satire about a ruler
Information spread on purpose to shape beliefs, often by misleading
A list of club members
check.why: Propaganda aims to shape what people believe. Ford's series used the Protocols this way.

check.q: Why did Ford's name help the forgery spread, according to the reading?
choices: He had studied Russian history
His fame and success made readers trust him, though that had nothing to do with the truth
He was a lawyer in the Bern trial
He had discovered Joly's book
check.why: The reading says readers trusted Ford because of his success, which lent the forgery credibility it did not earn.

lessons.title: Ford's Apology of 1927
lessons.mainIdea: A libel suit pushed Ford to sign a public apology in 1927, but the books his paper made kept spreading.
reading: In the 1920s the Dearborn Independent also attacked Aaron Sapiro, a Jewish lawyer who organized farmers' cooperatives. Sapiro sued Ford for *libel*, meaning printing false statements that damage someone's reputation. The trial in 1927 ended in a mistrial. Before a new trial could begin, Ford decided to settle the matter.

Ford signed a public statement dated 30 June 1927. It was drafted by Louis Marshall, a leader of the American Jewish Committee, and Ford accepted it without changes. In it Ford apologized to Jewish people, said he withdrew the attacks, and said he had not known the details of what his paper printed. At the end of 1927 the paper stopped publishing.

Historians debate how sincere the apology was. Ford owned the paper, and many doubt he did not know what it said. Also, copies of The International Jew kept circulating abroad, especially in Germany. In 1938, on his 75th birthday, Ford accepted a high honor from Nazi Germany, the Grand Cross of the German Eagle.

A *retraction* is a public statement taking back something said or printed. Ford's retraction shows both the power and the limits of correcting the record. It was real and public. It did not recall the books already printed or the ideas already planted.

words.d: printing false statements that damage a person's reputation
a trial that ends without a verdict and may have to be held again
a public statement taking back something that was said or printed

look.title: Ford's Statement, in Summary
look.text: Ford said he regretted that his paper had been used to spread charges against Jews, apologized for the harm done, and promised the attacks would end. He said he had not known the details of what was printed.
look.cite: Henry Ford, public statement of apology, dated 30 June 1927, drafted by Louis Marshall of the American Jewish Committee
look.prompt: Ford owned and funded the paper. How believable is the claim that he did not know what it printed? What evidence would help you decide?

check.q: What pushed Ford toward his 1927 apology?
choices: Aaron Sapiro's libel suit against him
The Bern trial verdict
An order from Congress
A letter from Philip Graves
check.why: Sapiro's libel suit ended in a mistrial, and Ford signed the apology before a new trial.

check.q: Who drafted the statement that Ford signed?
choices: Philip Graves
Judge Walter Meyer
Louis Marshall of the American Jewish Committee
Sergei Nilus
check.why: Louis Marshall drafted the statement, and Ford accepted it without changes.

check.q: Why do historians say the apology had limits?
choices: Ford never signed it
Copies of The International Jew kept circulating, and many doubt Ford's claim he did not know
It was printed only in Russian
It praised the Protocols
check.why: The books kept spreading abroad, and historians question Ford's claim of ignorance about his own paper.

lessons.title: The Forgery in Nazi Germany
lessons.mainIdea: Nazi leaders used the Protocols as propaganda, helping build the hatred that led to the Holocaust.
reading: In Germany after World War I, the Protocols found eager readers among people looking for someone to blame for defeat and hard times. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Nazi writer Alfred Rosenberg introduced Adolf Hitler to the text in the early 1920s. The Nazi party published at least 23 editions of it between 1919 and 1939.

Some German newspapers fought back. In 1924 the Frankfurter Zeitung, a respected paper, exposed the Protocols as a fraud. But after the Nazis took power in 1933, independent voices were silenced. The Protocols was even used in some German schools. Once they took power, they could print it with the full weight of the state behind it.

The forgery gave Nazi *ideology* a false story of a hidden enemy. An ideology is a set of ideas that a movement uses to explain the world and justify its actions. The Nazi state used that story to justify taking away Jewish people's rights, property and safety.

The end of that road was the *Holocaust*, the murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during World War II. A forged document did not cause the Holocaust by itself. But historians see it as one of the lies that prepared many people to accept persecution. The people harmed, not the forgers, are the center of this history.

words.d: a set of ideas a movement uses to explain the world and justify its actions
the murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during World War II
cruel and unfair treatment of people because of who they are or what they believe

look.title: A Museum's Summary
look.text: The Holocaust Memorial Museum explains that the Nazis promoted the Protocols to justify persecuting Jews, publishing many editions and using it in some schools, even though it had long been exposed as a forgery.
look.cite: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Protocols of the Elders of Zion'
look.prompt: The forgery had been exposed in 1921 and again in 1924. Why might a government keep using a text it could know was fake?

check.q: Who introduced Hitler to the Protocols in the early 1920s, according to the museum?
choices: Henry Ford
Maurice Joly
Philip Graves
Alfred Rosenberg
check.why: The Holocaust Memorial Museum says Alfred Rosenberg introduced Hitler to the text.

check.q: Which German paper exposed the Protocols as a fraud in 1924?
choices: Znamya
The Dearborn Independent
The Times
The Frankfurter Zeitung
check.why: The reading says the Frankfurter Zeitung exposed it in 1924, before the Nazis took power.

check.q: What is an ideology?
choices: A set of ideas a movement uses to explain the world and justify its actions
A court's final decision
A document made to deceive
A secret police force
check.why: An ideology is a movement's set of explaining ideas. The Protocols gave Nazi ideology a false hidden enemy.

lessons.title: A Lie That Keeps Returning
lessons.mainIdea: Though proven false for over a century, the Protocols still circulates, sometimes with the villain renamed.
reading: In 1964 a subcommittee of the United States Senate Judiciary Committee printed a report on the Protocols. Its title called the text a fabricated historic document. Even at the height of the Cold War, members of Congress put on record that the Protocols was fake and traced how it had spread.

Yet the text never went away. It is still printed and still shared online in many languages today. Human rights groups and Holocaust museums continue to track it. A lie that has been disproved can keep moving if people pass it on without checking where it came from. That is called *misinformation* when it is shared by mistake, and *disinformation* when it is spread on purpose.

Sometimes the Protocols returns in a new costume. Some writers keep the text but say it is really about a different secret group, such as the Illuminati. The writer Bill Cooper reprinted it in his 1991 book Behold a Pale Horse, a case this course studies in Unit 17. Many of Cooper's readers care about real government secrets, and some of those secrets are documented.

But renaming the villain does not change the text's history. It is still Joly's satire, rewritten by a forger to target Jews, and still the document the Nazis used. A reader can take real questions about secrecy seriously and still refuse to pass on a known forgery.

words.d: false information shared by people who do not know it is false
false information spread on purpose to deceive
made up or invented, especially to deceive

look.title: Same Text, New Label
look.text: A post online shares a long passage and says: This old document explains everything about the secret elite who run the world. It gives no author, no date and no place of first printing. A reader notices that the passage matches, in order, a text historians traced to Joly's 1864 satire.
look.prompt: The post never names Jews. Does that make it harmless to share? Use the words disinformation and fabricated in your answer.

check.q: What did a U.S. Senate subcommittee do in 1964?
choices: It banned all secret societies
It held that the Protocols were genuine
It printed a report calling the Protocols a fabricated document
It put Henry Ford on trial
check.why: The 1964 Senate Judiciary subcommittee print called the Protocols a fabricated historic document.

check.q: What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
choices: Misinformation is always spoken; disinformation is always printed
Misinformation is shared by mistake; disinformation is spread on purpose
They mean exactly the same thing
Disinformation is true; misinformation is false
check.why: The reading defines misinformation as false information shared by mistake and disinformation as spread on purpose.

check.q: Why does renaming the villain not make the Protocols a different document?
choices: Because its history as Joly's satire rewritten to target Jews stays the same
Because the Illuminati wrote it
Because Bill Cooper wrote the original
Because the Senate approved the new version
check.why: The reading says the text's origin and use against Jews do not change when the label changes.

lessons.title: Answering a Forgery With Care
lessons.mainIdea: The best answers to a hate forgery are checking its source, showing the evidence, and remembering the people it harmed.
reading: Graves, the Bern witnesses and the Frankfurter Zeitung reporters all did the same basic thing. They asked where the text came from and showed the answer. That is the heart of *source criticism*, the historian's habit of asking who made a document, when, where, how and why, before trusting it.

Careful people also avoid spreading the harm. Teachers who study the Protocols show only short matching lines next to Joly, and only to prove the copying. They do not hand out the full text. Repeating a hateful claim, even to argue with it, can plant it in new minds. Pointing to the evidence is safer than repeating the lie.

Center the people who were harmed. Jewish families in Russia, Germany and elsewhere lived with the fear and violence this text helped stir up. Honor also the people who stood up: Graves and his source, the Swiss Jewish groups who went to court, Louis Marshall and Aaron Sapiro in America, and the German reporters of 1924.

Finally, learn the pattern. Many forgeries follow the same shape: a secret meeting, a hidden group, a plan to rule the world, and no way to check the source. When you meet that shape, you can slow down, ask the source questions, and look for the original. That is a skill, and it grows with practice.

words.d: the habit of asking who made a document, when, where, how and why, before trusting it
the known history of a document: where it came from and who has held it
a shape or set of features that repeats across many cases

look.title: Five Source Questions
look.text: Who made this? When and where was it first printed? How did it reach me? Why might someone want me to believe it? Can I find the original, or an older text it copies? A student uses these five questions on a viral page that claims to reveal the secret minutes of a world meeting.
look.prompt: Which of the five questions would have exposed the Protocols fastest? Explain how Graves answered that question in 1921.

check.q: What is source criticism?
choices: Saying bad things about a writer
Copying a source into a report
Asking who made a document, when, where, how and why, before trusting it
Choosing only sources you agree with
check.why: Source criticism is the historian's set of questions about a document's origin and purpose.

check.q: Why do careful teachers show only short matching lines of the Protocols?
choices: Because the full text is lost
Because the goal is to prove the copying without spreading the hateful text
Because it is too hard to read
Because the law forbids any quotation
check.why: The reading says repeating hate can plant it in new minds, so teachers show only paired lines as proof.

check.q: Which set of features is the common pattern of such forgeries?
choices: A named author, a clear date and a library record
A court verdict and an appeal
A satire that openly names its target
A secret meeting, a hidden group, a plan to rule the world, and no checkable source
check.why: The reading lists this shape so readers can recognize it and slow down.

review.q: What was Maurice Joly's 1864 Dialogue in Hell mainly about?
choices: A secret Jewish council
The Russian Revolution
The founding of Switzerland
The rule of Emperor Napoleon III
review.why: Joly's satire criticized Napoleon III and never mentioned Jews.

review.q: In what year and city was the Protocols first printed?
choices: 1903, St. Petersburg
1864, Brussels
1921, London
1935, Bern
review.why: The newspaper Znamya printed it in St. Petersburg in 1903.

review.q: What method did Philip Graves use to show the copying?
choices: He tested the ink in a lab
He interviewed the elders
He printed matching passages in parallel columns
He asked a court to decide
review.why: Graves set Joly's lines beside the Protocols so readers could see the match.

review.q: Which statement about who made the Protocols is most accurate?
choices: Joly wrote it himself in 1864
It is a forgery, but historians still debate who made it
It is proven that Golovinski wrote it alone
Graves wrote it to sell newspapers
review.why: The forgery is settled; the forger's identity is still debated among historians.

review.q: What did the 1937 Bern appeal decide?
choices: That the trashy literature law did not fit, without finding the text genuine
That the Protocols were genuine
That Joly was guilty of libel
That Ford must pay damages
review.why: The appeal turned on a point of law and made no finding that the Protocols were real.

review.q: Henry Ford's 1927 apology came after which event?
choices: The Bern verdict
Graves's death
Aaron Sapiro's libel suit ended in a mistrial
The Nazi party took power
review.why: Ford signed the apology after the Sapiro libel trial ended in a mistrial.

review.q: How did Nazi Germany use the Protocols?
choices: It banned the text as a forgery
It published many editions and used it as propaganda, even in some schools
It sent it to Bern for testing
It used it only as a history lesson on forgery
review.why: The Holocaust Memorial Museum reports at least 23 Nazi editions and use in some schools.

review.q: A writer reprints the Protocols but says it is really about the Illuminati. What is the best response?
choices: It becomes a new, genuine document
It is harmless because Jews are not named
It must be true if it has been reprinted
The text is still a forgery copied from Joly and used to target Jews
review.why: Renaming the villain does not change the text's origin or the harm it was made to do.
